original_question: Can one explicitly compute, program, and publish tables of parity-independent osp(1|2) 6-j^S symbols for low spins (for example up to spin 20) from the general formulas cited by the paper, so that low-spin calculations can test candidate triangle-sum-rule identities and reveal patterns among the expansion coefficients x?
target_in_paper: The paper’s central open problem is to complete the “ultimate identification” over the binomial basis (c0+d0^2)^(Ω-m)(d0^2)^m by determining the unknown polynomials P^ω(λ,κ) and their expansion coefficients x, in order to obtain a genuine osp(1|2) super-triangle sum rule for the parity-independent 6-j^S symbols, with supertriangles Δ^S rather than the su(2)/su_q(2) triangles ∇.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly points to the parity-independent osp(1|2) 6-j^S calculus, the search for an osp(1|2) triangle/super-triangle sum rule, and the importance of the unknown expansion coefficients x. It also reasonably treats explicit low-spin computation as possible evidence-gathering for the unresolved problem.
missing_details: The paper’s actual unknowns are not the low-spin 6-j^S symbols themselves, but the polynomials P^ω(λ,κ) and their expansion coefficients x over the binomials (c0+d0^2)^(Ω-m)(d0^2)^m.
The official goal is not to tabulate symbols up to a cutoff such as spin 20, but to prove a veritable osp(1|2) super-triangle sum rule analytically.
The question must specify that the wanted identity is obtained by identifying two intrinsic-operator expressions for a triple tensor product, in direct analogy with the su(2) derivation.
The paper insists that the osp(1|2) identity must involve supertriangles Δ^S, not the usual ∇ triangles from su(2)/su_q(2).
The earlier relation attributed to Zeng is explicitly not the target; the paper says it is still far from the ‘veritable’ osp(1|2) triangle sum rule sought here.
The dependence on parity/integrality cases is missing: Appendix B distinguishes ω=p (integral) and ω=π (half-integral).
The parameters λ and κ, and the basis index m with exponent Ω-m, should be named, because x depends on them.
The draft omits Conjecture 1: the coefficients x are conjectured to be integers.
The draft does not say that the paper works in the parity-independent osp(1|2) Racah/Wigner calculus for admissible couplings; that admissibility is implicit in any stand-alone formulation.

The computational aims ‘program’, ‘publish tables’, and ‘up to spin 20’ are not stated anywhere as the paper’s official problem, so keeping them as the main question broadens and shifts the paper’s intent.
No ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree, or nilpotency hypotheses are part of this paper’s problem; importing such language would be misleading here.
refined_question: For admissible parity-independent osp(1|2) 6-j^S symbols, can one determine the unknown polynomials P^ω(λ,κ) (with ω=p in the integral case and ω=π in the half-integral case) and their binomial expansion coefficients x_m^ω(λ,κ) in the basis (c0+d0^2)^(Ω-m)(d0^2)^m, so as to complete the intrinsic-operator identification of the two triple-tensor-product expressions and thereby prove a genuine osp(1|2) super-triangle sum rule—written with supertriangles Δ^S rather than the su(2)/su_q(2) triangles ∇—for the parity-independent 6-j^S coefficients?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently: can one find a general closed formula for the integer coefficients x_m^ω(λ,κ) appearing in the expansion of P^ω(λ,κ) over the binomials (c0+d0^2)^(Ω-m)(d0^2)^m, since this unresolved ‘ultimate identification’ is exactly the remaining step before the sought osp(1|2) super-triangle sum rule can be obtained?
justification: The draft captures the computational shadow of the paper’s problem, but not the problem itself. The paper does not present low-spin tables as the goal; it presents the unresolved analytic identification problem whose solution would yield a veritable osp(1|2) super-triangle sum rule. The abstract already states the real unknowns—polynomials P and coefficients x—together with the need for supertriangles Δ^S and the integrality conjecture for x. Section 3 shows, in the su(2) model case, that triangle sum rules arise by identifying two formulas for a triple tensor product. Appendix B records the P^ω(λ,κ) framework and parity split in which x lives, and Appendix C explains why the earlier Zeng-type relation is not the intended target.
